how_it_works.text: Chandra uses four nested pairs of grazing-incidence mirrors, coated with iridium, to deflect X-rays that would otherwise pass straight through or be absorbed. The mirror shells focus incoming photons onto a 9.2-metre optical bench, where either the ACIS CCD camera or the HRC microchannel-plate detector records an image, while the HETGS and LETG gratings spread the X-rays into spectra. Because Earth's atmosphere blocks X-rays, the observatory flies in a highly elliptical orbit that reaches roughly 139,000 km above the surface.

why_important.text: Chandra was the first X-ray telescope to deliver sub-arcsecond imaging, letting astronomers resolve structures that earlier missions could only blur together. It has mapped million-degree gas in galaxy clusters, traced shock fronts in supernova remnants, measured matter falling toward black holes, and shown how dark matter separates from ordinary gas during cluster collisions. Those observations underpin much of modern high-energy astrophysics and complement the infrared and visible-light work of Hubble and Webb.

status.text: NASA lists Chandra as an active mission as of the agency page's 14 April 2026 update. The Chandra X-ray Center, operated for NASA by the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, continues to run flight operations and science activities, and the observatory remains in its highly elliptical orbit.

how_it_works.text: Clementine was built around a small, lightweight bus and carried 15 advanced flight-test components alongside nine science instruments. Its lunar mapping payload combined an ultraviolet/visible camera, a near-infrared camera and a laser altimeter, which together recorded surface colour, mineral signatures and topography. Two further cameras served as star trackers for the spacecraft's autonomous attitude system. The Naval Research Laboratory designed, integrated and flew the spacecraft for the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization, while NASA provided science oversight and investigators.

why_important.text: Clementine produced the first near-global multispectral map of the Moon and the first global topographic map from lunar orbit, giving scientists a consistent data set for studying the crust's composition and relief. Its bistatic radar experiment returned signals consistent with water ice trapped in a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole, a result that reshaped lunar polar science and motivated later ice-hunting missions. The project also became an early template for the 'faster, better, cheaper' approach that shaped NASA's Discovery programme.

status.text: Clementine's mission ended on 8 August 1994, after a thruster fault and a power-system failure prevented the planned Geographos flyby and drained the spacecraft's battery. Lunar gravity had already pushed it into a heliocentric orbit on 20 July 1994, and controllers briefly regained contact between 20 February and 10 May 1995. The spacecraft has not been operated since.

how_it_works.text: CloudSat carried a single instrument, the Cloud Profiling Radar, a nadir-pointing 94 GHz W-band radar that measured the strength of backscattered pulses at successive heights through a cloud. That produced vertical slices of cloud structure with about 500 m resolution, revealing where liquid water, ice and precipitation sit inside a cloud rather than only how its top appears. The spacecraft flew in a 705 km, 98.2-degree sun-synchronous orbit as part of the A-Train, and had a launch mass of 847 kg.

why_important.text: CloudSat was the first satellite to profile the vertical structure of clouds across the globe, filling a gap previously covered only by cloud-top imagers and ground-based radars. Its measurements of cloud water content, snowfall and precipitation helped test and improve the cloud parameterisations used in climate and weather models. The mission's long global record continues to support studies of how cloud systems vary with season, region and climate.

status.text: NASA decommissioned CloudSat on 20 December 2023, when radar science operations concluded. The spacecraft completed final orbit-lowering manoeuvres and was passivated in April 2024, leaving it inactive and awaiting disposal. Its radar data remain archived and continue to be used for climate and weather research.

how_it_works.text: Cluster II is a set of four identical spinning spacecraft that fly in a tetrahedral formation, so the same region of near-Earth space is sampled at four points at once. Their orbits are highly eccentric and near-polar, with a nominal perigee of about 4 Earth radii, apogee of about 19.6 Earth radii, a period near 57 hours and an inclination of about 90.7 degrees. Each spacecraft carries a matched suite of magnetometers, electric-field sensors, wave receivers and particle spectrometers, and the separation between the four is adjusted to match the scale of the plasma structures being studied.

why_important.text: Before Cluster, most magnetospheric measurements came from single spacecraft, which could not separate spatial structure from temporal change. Flying four identical observatories in a known formation let researchers resolve boundaries, currents, waves and turbulence in three dimensions and trace how solar-wind energy enters Earth's magnetosphere. The mission operated for more than two decades, supported space-weather modelling, and ended with the first repeated targeted reentries of a multi-spacecraft science constellation.

status.text: Cluster's science operations are complete. The four satellites were disposed of through targeted reentries over the South Pacific: Salsa on 8 September 2024, Rumba on 22 October 2025, Samba on 31 August 2026 and Tango on 1 September 2026. ESA describes the campaign as the first repeated, controlled reentry of a multi-spacecraft science mission.

how_it_works.text: Curiosity is a car-sized rover that landed in Gale Crater using a rocket-powered descent stage, which lowered it to the surface on a tether before flying away. It moves on six wheels with a rocker-bogie suspension and draws power from a radioisotope thermoelectric generator rather than solar panels. Its instruments include the SAM and CheMin laboratories for analysing drilled rock powder, the ChemCam laser spectrometer and Mastcam cameras on the mast, the APXS and MAHLI sensors on the robotic arm, and the DAN, REMS and RAD environment instruments.

why_important.text: Curiosity's central question was whether Gale Crater ever offered conditions that could have supported microbial life. The mission established that the crater once held a long-lived freshwater lake with the chemical ingredients and energy sources needed for life, detected complex organic molecules in ancient mudstones, and documented how Martian climate and habitability changed over time. Its radiation and weather measurements also inform planning for human exploration.

status.text: Curiosity remains active in Gale Crater. NASA reported on 26 August 2026 that the rover had gained about 1 km of elevation during its climb of Mount Sharp, and the mission continues to study progressively younger sedimentary layers.

how_it_works.text: CYGNSS uses eight small observatories in low Earth orbit, each carrying a Delay Doppler Mapping Instrument that listens for GPS signals reflected from the ocean surface. The shape and strength of the reflected signal depend on surface roughness, which is used to retrieve wind speed beneath the storm. Each satellite uses under 60 W of power and weighs less than 30 kg, deploying solar panels after launch, and the constellation's orbits are arranged to revisit tropical storms frequently.

why_important.text: CYGNSS was designed to measure ocean surface winds inside tropical cyclones, where heavy rain and cloud tops block or obscure visible and infrared images. By flying a constellation of small satellites, it increases the number of observations of a storm's inner core and helps forecasters track intensification, complementing larger weather satellites and aircraft reconnaissance.

status.text: CYGNSS is listed by NASA as an active mission and continues to operate in extended mission. Its data are used in research on tropical cyclones, ocean surface winds and air-sea exchange.

how_it_works.text: Danuri, also called the Korea Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter, is a 678 kg spacecraft about 1.8 by 2.1 by 2.3 m in size. It reached the Moon on a ballistic lunar transfer that uses solar, Earth and lunar gravity rather than a direct braking burn, then entered a 100 km circular polar orbit. Its six payloads include Korean cameras, a magnetometer and a gamma-ray spectrometer, together with NASA's ShadowCam, which is sensitive enough to image permanently shadowed polar terrain using light reflected from nearby crater walls.

why_important.text: Danuri is the Republic of Korea's first mission beyond Earth orbit and its first lunar orbiter. It gives Korean engineers and scientists operational experience in lunar trajectory design, deep-space communications and payload operations, while its imagery, magnetic and gamma-ray data add to international lunar datasets. ShadowCam's images of permanently shadowed regions support planning for future polar landings, including Artemis.

status.text: Danuri is active. KARI states that the mission was extended by two years and is scheduled to continue science operations through 2027.

what_is_it.text: Dawn was NASA's first truly interplanetary spaceship capable of visiting, orbiting, and exploring two distinct extraterrestrial bodies in deep space. Flown under NASA's Discovery program, Dawn spent extended years exploring the giant asteroid Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter to investigate the conditions present at the birth of the solar system.

how_it_works.text: Dawn relied on innovative xenon ion propulsion thrusters, which accelerated ionized xenon gas electrostatically to achieve exceptionally high propellant efficiency and execute complex orbital rendezvous at multiple planetary targets. Large deployable solar panels powered the ion engines and payload, which included framing cameras, a visible and infrared mapping spectrometer, and a gamma ray and neutron detector.

why_important.text: Dawn became the first human spacecraft to orbit an object in the main asteroid belt (Vesta in 2011) and the first to visit and orbit a dwarf planet (Ceres in 2015). It provided evidence of ancient interior heating and fluid flow on Ceres, examined clues of long-standing internal energy and potential habitability, and photographed dramatic bright sodium carbonate salt deposits inside Occator Crater on Ceres.

status.text: Dawn completed its mission successfully after exhausting its hydrazine attitude-control propellant on October 31 - November 1, 2018. Having met all planetary protection requirements, the silent spacecraft remains in a stable, unpowered perpetual orbit around dwarf planet Ceres.

how_it_works.text: Deep Impact flew two connected spacecraft: a 370 kg copper impactor and a 650 kg flyby bus. The impactor was released about 24 hours before encounter and struck comet Tempel 1 at 10.2 km/s, while the flyby watched from a safe distance with its High Resolution Instrument, Medium Resolution Instrument and infrared spectrometer. The copper mass was chosen so that the impactor's own material would not confuse measurements of the comet's composition.

why_important.text: The collision excavated material from beneath Tempel 1's surface, allowing the flyby to analyse fresh cometary ice, dust and organic compounds and to watch how a crater forms on a low-gravity body. The experiment produced the first direct look inside a comet nucleus and linked the mission to later studies of cometary structure and the delivery of volatiles to the inner solar system.

status.text: Deep Impact's primary mission ended after the Tempel 1 encounter, and the spacecraft was then reused as EPOXI for a flyby of comet Hartley 2 in 2010 and other observations. NASA lost contact with the spacecraft on 16 September 2013 and declared the mission complete.

how_it_works.text: Deep Space 1 was built around a xenon ion propulsion system that used electricity from solar arrays to accelerate ions and produce a very small but continuous thrust. The 30 cm engine carried about 81.5 kg of xenon, and the spacecraft's total launch mass was 486.3 kg. It also flew an autonomous navigation package, AutoNav, that used camera images of asteroids and stars to steer the spacecraft without ground intervention, plus the MICAS camera/spectrometer and the PEPE plasma instrument.

why_important.text: Deep Space 1 was a technology demonstration that proved ion propulsion could serve as a primary deep-space propulsion system, and it validated autonomous optical navigation and miniaturised science instruments. Its encounters with asteroid Braille and comet Borrelly showed that these technologies could deliver real science, and the ion engine design became the basis for the propulsion used on Dawn.

status.text: Deep Space 1 completed its mission on 18 December 2001, after the Borrelly flyby. The spacecraft was intentionally shut down and remains inactive in heliocentric orbit.

how_it_works.text: DSCOVR orbits the Sun-Earth L1 point about 1.5 million km sunward of Earth, where it can sample the solar wind before it reaches the planet. Its PlasMag suite combines a Faraday cup and a magnetometer to measure the speed, density, temperature and magnetic field of the incoming plasma. A pair of Earth-viewing instruments, EPIC and NISTAR, look back at the fully illuminated Earth to image the disk and measure reflected sunlight and emitted radiation.

why_important.text: DSCOVR is NOAA's operational real-time solar-wind monitor and the successor to NASA's ACE at L1. Its measurements give forecasters roughly 15 to 60 minutes of warning before a solar-wind disturbance reaches Earth, supporting geomagnetic storm watches and alerts that protect satellites, power grids, aviation and GPS users. EPIC's images also provide a continuous view of the sunlit Earth for climate and cloud studies.

status.text: DSCOVR is listed by NASA as an active mission and continues to operate at L1 under NOAA. NOAA took over routine operations on 28 October 2015.

what_is_it.text: The Apollo 15 Lunar Module 'Falcon' (LM-10) was the fourth crewed vehicle to land on the Moon, transporting Commander David R. Scott and Lunar Module Pilot James B. Irwin to the surface on July 30, 1971. In addition to housing and landing the astronauts, the spacecraft delivered the first Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV) and the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP) to the Hadley-Apennine landing site for extended scientific investigations.

how_it_works.text: The Lunar Module was a two-stage spacecraft with a total mass of 16,430 kg at launch. The descent stage (dry mass 2,797 kg, 8,873 kg propellant) was an octagonal prism measuring 4.2 meters across and 1.7 meters thick, equipped with a 45,000 N deep-throttling ablative rocket engine, four landing gear legs spanning 9.4 meters, silver-zinc batteries, and storage bays for the LRV and ALSEP instruments. The ascent stage (dry mass 2,385 kg, 2,375 kg propellant) housed the 6.65 cubic meter pressurized crew cabin, Apollo guidance computer, 15,000 N constant-thrust rocket engine, reaction control thrusters, and S-band and VHF antennas. Power for surface science was supplied by a SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generator producing ~70 W DC from a plutonium-238 capsule.

why_important.text: Apollo 15 marked the first extended scientific expedition to the Moon and the first deployment of the Lunar Roving Vehicle. The crew completed three moonwalk EVAs totaling 18 hours and 35 minutes, traversed 27.9 km across Hadley Rille and the Apennine Mountains, and collected 77.31 kg of rock and soil samples, including a core drill sample from three meters depth. Commander Scott also performed the famous televised demonstration of a hammer and feather dropping at identical rates in the lunar vacuum.

status.text: The LM ascent stage lifted off from the Moon on August 2, 1971 at 17:11:22 UT, docked with the CSM, and was jettisoned on August 3, intentionally impacting the Moon at 26.36 N, 0.25 E. The descent stage remains at the landing site (26.13239 N, 3.63330 E). The ALSEP scientific station transmitted surface geophysical data continuously until all Apollo ALSEP stations were officially shut down on September 30, 1977.

what_is_it.text: The Apollo 12 Lunar Module 'Intrepid' (LM-6) was the second crewed vehicle to land on the Moon, carrying Commander Charles 'Pete' Conrad and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean to Oceanus Procellarum on November 19, 1969. The spacecraft demonstrated pinpoint lunar landing accuracy by touching down within approximately 180 meters of the robotic Surveyor 3 lander and carried the first complete Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP).

how_it_works.text: The Lunar Module comprised an ascent stage (dry mass 2,383 kg, 2,375 kg propellant) and a descent stage (dry mass 2,118 kg, 8,359 kg propellant) with a total mass of 15,235 kg. The descent stage used a 45,000 N throttleable rocket engine for powered descent and landed on four gear legs spanning 9.4 meters. The ascent stage featured a 6.65 cubic meter crew compartment, a 15,000 N constant-thrust ascent engine, S-band parabolic antenna, VHF transceivers, Apollo guidance computer, and silver-zinc batteries. The ALSEP instruments were powered by a 17 kg SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generator containing a 4 kg plutonium-238 capsule producing ~70 W DC.

why_important.text: Apollo 12 proved that pinpoint precision landings on the Moon were achievable, landing within walking distance (180 meters) of the Surveyor 3 probe. Astronauts performed two moonwalks totaling 7 hours and 45 minutes, gathered 34.35 kg of lunar samples, retrieved ~10 kg of Surveyor 3 components (including its TV camera) to test prolonged space exposure, and deployed the first nuclear-powered geophysical ALSEP station. Upon jettison, the ascent stage's deliberate lunar impact produced the first recorded artificial moonquake.

status.text: After 31 hours and 31 minutes on the lunar surface, the ascent stage lifted off on November 20, 1969 at 14:25:47 UT, docked with the CSM, and was jettisoned at 20:21:30 UT. It intentionally crashed into the Moon at 3.94 S, 338.80 E (~60 km from the landing site). The descent stage remains at Oceanus Procellarum (3.0128 S, 23.4219 W). The ALSEP geophysical station transmitted science data until it was shut down on September 30, 1977.

what_is_it.text: Spirit (MER-A) was one of NASA's twin Mars Exploration Rovers sent to explore the Red Planet as a robotic field geologist. Launched in 2003, Spirit touched down on January 3, 2004 at Gusev Crater, an ancient crater suspected to have once harbored an impact-basin lake, in search of clues about the historical presence of liquid water on Mars.

how_it_works.text: Spirit was an autonomous six-wheeled rover powered by multi-panel solar arrays. It featured an articulated rocker-bogie mobility suspension to traverse rough terrain, a mast-mounted Panoramic Camera (Pancam) with multi-spectral color filters, and a deployable robotic instrument arm to position scientific sensors in direct contact with Martian rocks and soils.

why_important.text: Spirit provided groundbreaking evidence confirming that liquid water was long-standing on ancient Mars. Operating for more than six years across a mission originally planned for 90 days, Spirit drove 4.8 miles (7.7 kilometers), scaled the Columbia Hills, and discovered extensive silica deposits that pointed to past hydrothermal activity and volcanic steam vents.

status.text: Spirit completed its primary mission and extended investigations across over 2,200 sols, driving 4.8 miles (7.7 km). The rover became lodged in soft soil at 'Troy' in 2009 and served as a stationary science platform until contact was lost in March 2010 following winter power decline. NASA formally concluded the mission in 2010.

what_is_it.text: Viking 1 was the first NASA spacecraft to achieve a successful soft landing on Mars, providing humanity's first extended operational look at the Red Planet's surface. Launched on August 20, 1975, the mission consisted of an orbiter to map the planet from space and a lander equipped with a biological laboratory to conduct direct in-situ searches for signs of Martian life.

how_it_works.text: The composite Viking 1 spacecraft weighed 7,776 pounds (3,527 kg), comprising a 5,157-pound (2,339 kg) solar-powered orbiter and a 2,156-pound (978 kg) lander powered by two SNAP-19 radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs). Launched by a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket, the orbiter conducted atmospheric and surface mapping, while the lander deployed an aeroshell, parachute, and terminal descent engines before using a robotic sampler arm to deliver soil to onboard chemical and biological analysis chambers.

why_important.text: Viking 1 made history on July 20, 1976 by successfully landing on Chryse Planitia and returning the first color images, panoramas, and meteorological data from the Martian surface. The mission returned over 50,000 orbiter images (mapping 97% of the surface) and 4,500 surface photos, revealing volcanic features, immense canyons, water-carved channels, and sulfur-rich soil, establishing the foundational baseline for modern Mars exploration.

status.text: Viking 1 completed its primary mission in November 1976 and continued through extended survey operations. The orbiter was deactivated on August 7, 1980 after exhausting attitude-control propellant during its 1,489th orbit. The lander, renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station in 1982, returned daily weather reports until November 11, 1982, when a flawed ground command permanently disrupted communications.

what_is_it.text: InSight (Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport) was a stationary NASA lander engineered to probe the deep interior structure of Mars. Part of NASA's Discovery program, the mission was designed to measure Mars' internal 'pulse' (seismology), 'temperature' (heat flow), and 'reflexes' (precession tracking) to uncover the formation and evolution of rocky planets in the inner solar system.

how_it_works.text: Derived from the flight-proven Mars Phoenix lander design, InSight utilized twin deployable UltraFlex solar arrays built by Lockheed Martin Space Systems. It was launched from California's Central Coast on an Atlas V-401 rocket alongside two MarCO technology-demonstration CubeSats. The lander featured a 5 foot 9 inch (1.8-meter) robotic instrument deployment arm that lifted its seismometer and heat flow probe from the deck and placed them directly onto the Martian ground.

why_important.text: InSight offered humanity's first comprehensive examination beneath the Martian crust, detecting hundreds of marsquakes and tracking seismic tremors caused by meteorite impacts that penetrated deep into the planet's mantle. It revealed the layered nature of Mars' interior, measured the depth of its crust and the size of its liquid metallic core, and captured the first audio recordings of Martian wind blowing across Elysium Planitia.

status.text: InSight landed safely on November 26, 2018 at Elysium Planitia (4.5 N, 135.9 E) and operated for over four years. On December 15, 2022, after thick Martian dust steadily covered its solar panels and diminished electrical output below operating thresholds, NASA announced the end of the mission.

what_is_it.text: NEAR Shoemaker (Near Earth Asteroid Rendezvous) was the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid and the first to soft-land on one. Flown as the inaugural mission of NASA's Discovery program, the robotic explorer rendezvoused with the near-Earth asteroid 433 Eros to gather data on its physical properties, mineralogy, surface morphology, and magnetic field. It was later renamed in honor of renowned planetary geologist Eugene M. Shoemaker.

how_it_works.text: The spacecraft weighed 1,775 pounds (805 kg) and was launched by a Delta 7925-8 rocket. It was the first planetary mission to rely entirely on solar cells for electrical power beyond the orbit of Mars. Although not designed as a lander, NEAR possessed hydrazine attitude thrusters, guidance sensors, and an array of spectrometers, laser rangefinders, and imaging cameras that allowed controllers to guide it through a controlled 4 mph (6.4 km/h) touchdown onto the asteroid surface.

why_important.text: NEAR achieved an unprecedented series of firsts: the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid (February 14, 2000) and the first to touch down on one (February 12, 2001). It marked the first time an American spacecraft was the first in human history to land on an extraterrestrial celestial body. The probe mapped over 70% of Eros, returned 160,000 images, and survived touchdown to beam gamma-ray surface spectroscopy data back to Earth for two weeks.

status.text: NEAR successfully touched down on asteroid 433 Eros just south of Himeros on February 12, 2001. It operated on the surface until February 28, 2001, when extreme surface temperatures (minus 279 degrees Fahrenheit / minus 173 degrees Celsius) drained operating batteries. The probe rests permanently on Eros.

what_is_it.text: Pioneer 10 (Pioneer-F) was NASA's trailblazing first robotic mission to the outer planets. Launched in March 1972, the spacecraft achieved an unmatched series of deep-space exploration milestones, becoming the first probe to venture beyond Mars, the first to traverse the main asteroid belt, the first to conduct a close flyby of Jupiter, and the first human-built craft placed on an escape trajectory out of the solar system.

how_it_works.text: Weighing 569 pounds (258 kilograms), Pioneer 10 was boosted by a three-stage Atlas Centaur rocket with a TE-M-364-4 upper stage to a record escape velocity of 32,110 mph (51,682 km/h). Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to rely exclusively on nuclear electrical power, driven by twin SNAP-19 radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) generating ~140 W during its Jupiter flyby. It operated with spin stabilization and carried an array of magnetic, plasma, and imaging photopolarimeter instruments alongside an iconic gold-anodized pictorial plaque.

why_important.text: Pioneer 10 revolutionized planetary science by revealing that Jupiter is predominantly a liquid planet encased in intense trapped-radiation belts and a massive magnetic tail stretching nearly 800 million kilometers. In June 1983, it crossed the orbit of Neptune to become the first human-made object to venture beyond the outermost known planet, operating for over three decades across a mission planned for 21 months.

status.text: NASA maintained routine communications with Pioneer 10 until March 31, 1997. Ground antennas received the spacecraft's final faint radio signal on January 23, 2003, at a distance of 7.6 billion miles (12.23 billion kilometers) from Earth. Pioneer 10 is currently drifting silently into interstellar space toward the red star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus.

what_is_it.text: The Kepler Space Telescope was NASA’s first dedicated planet-hunting mission, assigned to survey our region of the Milky Way galaxy for Earth-sized exoplanets orbiting within stellar habitable zones. Operating in an Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit, Kepler and its second-act extended mission, K2, surveyed more than 500,000 stars over nine years in deep space.

how_it_works.text: The spacecraft was built around a single primary instrument: a specialized 3-foot (1-meter) aperture Schmidt telescope equipped with a 4-foot 7-inch (1.4-meter) primary mirror and a 95-megapixel image sensor array—the largest digital camera array launched into outer space at that time. Kepler detected planets by observing transits, recording tiny periodic dips in stellar brightness. When two of four reaction wheels failed in 2013, engineers used solar photon pressure to balance the telescope's pointing, initiating the extended K2 mission.

why_important.text: Kepler revolutionized astronomy by confirming more than 2,600 exoplanets and proving that planets outnumber stars in our galaxy. Its observations revealed that 20 to 50 percent of stars visible in the night sky likely host small, rocky planets in their habitable zones. Kepler discovered the first multi-planet transiting systems (Kepler-9 and Kepler-11) and demonstrated that worlds between the size of Earth and Neptune are common throughout the Milky Way.

status.text: After nine years of operations, Kepler exhausted its attitude-control fuel needed for further science observations. NASA officially retired the spacecraft on October 30, 2018, leaving it safely parked in its Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit.

timeline.description: Launched aboard a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station.

timeline.title: First Exoplanet Discoveries
timeline.description: NASA announced Kepler's first five exoplanet detections (Kepler 4b through 8b).

timeline.description: Confirmed Kepler-9, the first planetary system with multiple planets transiting the same star.

timeline.title: Second Reaction Wheel Failure
timeline.description: Loss of second reaction wheel concluded prime mission; engineers devised solar-pressure pointing.

timeline.title: K2 Mission Initiated
timeline.description: Commenced K2 extended mission observing fields along the ecliptic plane across 19 campaigns.

timeline.description: NASA retired Kepler within its safe Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit upon fuel exhaustion.
